Neonates of Green iguana (Iguana iguana) emerge from eggs weighing approximately 9 grams [Wwb = approximately 9 grams], a modest initial wet weight that is notably smaller than the 90 grams sometimes cited in popular husbandry guides, which appears inconsistent with reported snout-vent lengths. This low birth mass reflects the considerable yolk reserves allocated during embryonic development, which sustain the hatchling through its first days of independent life. The age at birth, or incubation period, is approximately 105 days [ab = approximately 105 days] when eggs are incubated at a constant 30 °C [T = 30 °C], though natural nests with fluctuating thermal regimes may yield durations ranging from 90 to 120 days. Hatchlings emerge using a specialized egg caruncle to break through the leathery, parchment-like shell, a process known as shell pipping that precedes complete emergence from the nest cavity. The 9-gram birth weight places Iguana iguana among the heavier hatchling iguanids, a consequence of its relatively large egg size and the substantial energy reserves required to sustain the neonate during the critical period between nest emergence and the onset of active foraging, which typically occurs within the first week following eclosion.

Under field conditions averaging 27 °C [T = 27 °C], female Green iguanas become capable of first reproduction at an age of 1,095 days [tR = 1,095 days], a threshold reached considerably later than in smaller-bodied iguanid lizards such as those in the genus Anolis, where maturity can be attained within a single year. This delayed onset of reproduction is characteristic of a slow-paced life history strategy, wherein individuals prioritize somatic growth and skeletal development during their initial years. The reported maximum documented lifespan for this species under natural conditions is 7,227 days [am = 7,227 days], equivalent to nearly two decades, recorded in populations experiencing the same mean annual temperature of 27 °C at a temperature of 27 °C [T = 27 °C]. This extended longevity, among the greatest documented for any iguanid lizard, reflects the combined effects of large body size, low predation pressure on adults, and a seasonally stable environment that supports gradual tissue maintenance and repair.

Concerning body size at adulthood, female Green iguanas ultimately achieve a maximum wet weight of approximately 3,500 grams [Wwi = approximately 3,500 grams], a value derived from field studies of reproductively active individuals inhabiting dry forest regions where food availability is moderate. Some populations, particularly those occupying resource-rich neotropical lowland forests with abundant foliage and extended basking periods, can attain an even greater ultimate wet weight of 9,100 grams [Wwi = 9,100 grams] for the largest females, demonstrating substantial intraspecific variation in asymptotic mass that correlates strongly with local resource gradients. This considerable range in adult body mass is influenced by local forage availability, basking opportunity, and population density, with heavier females typically producing larger clutch sizes and exhibiting higher overall fecundity. The species exhibits marked sexual size dimorphism, with males regularly exceeding the upper end of this female weight range, frequently reaching 12,000 grams or more in prime lowland habitats.

Reproductive output in female Green iguanas is characterized by a single annual nesting event, with clutch sizes ranging from 20 to 71 eggs per clutch [N_R_i = 20 to 71 eggs per clutch]. This wide range reflects variation in female body condition and age, as larger, older females consistently deposit more eggs. The frequency of reproduction is one clutch per year [F_R_i = one clutch per year], a pattern consistent with the energetic demands of vitellogenesis and the seasonal availability of suitable nesting substrates. Under optimal thermal conditions of 30 °C [T = 30 °C], females deposit eggs in communal nesting sites on sandy beaches or riverbanks, excavating burrows up to two meters in length to protect the clutch from desiccation and thermal extremes. The total annual reproductive investment, while substantial in terms of egg mass relative to female body size, is heavily offset by high nest predation rates and significant hatchling mortality, with recruitment to the adult population estimated at less than five percent in most years.

The extended developmental trajectory of Green iguana is further illustrated by its age at first reproduction, which for females is approximately 3 years [tR = approximately 3 years] under field conditions averaging 27 °C [T = 27 °C]; this is a relatively rapid maturation compared to the species' overall lifespan. Juveniles grow rapidly during their first two years, transitioning from a primarily insectivorous diet to a fully herbivorous one as they mature, which supports the accumulation of body mass necessary for reproduction. The species demonstrates a classic slow-fast life-history continuum within squamates, with delayed maturity and extended lifespan traded off against high fecundity per reproductive event. Comparative data suggest that island populations of Iguana iguana may exhibit even longer lifespans and later ages at first reproduction than mainland counterparts, likely due to reduced predation pressure and more stable food supplies. The combination of high adult survival and low annual reproductive output positions this species as a classic K-selected reptile, in stark contrast to the high fecundity and early maturity observed in many smaller tropical lizards.
